headline: Recommended City Council adopt residential tax factor .997300 for FY2027 and accept $132,000 Harbor Walk and $124,300 Railroad Avenue state grants.
summary: The committee discussed shifting part of the tax levy between property classes and recommended a 1.03 CIP shift for FY2027. It recommended accepting several donations, a special budgetary transfer, and two state grants, with Councilor Page opposing the Harbor Walk grant. The $14,000 Mass Cultural Council grant was continued to November 5, 2026.
decisions: Recommended that the City Council adopt a residential tax classification factor of .997300, equal to a CIP shift of 1.03 for FY2027, by a 3-0 vote.
Recommended City Council approval of Special Budgetary Transfer #2027-SBT-3 of $389.76 to cover a salary shortfall, by a 3-0 vote.
Recommended City Council acceptance of $65.00 in cash donations to the Archives Department, by a 3-0 vote.
Recommended City Council acceptance of $3,720.01 in cash donations to Veterans Services, by a 3-0 vote.
Recommended City Council acceptance of a $100 donation to the Community Impact Unit, by a 3-0 vote.
Recommended City Council acceptance of a framed portrait of former City Clerk Joanne M. Senos valued at about $150, by a 2-0 vote with Councilor Grow recused.
Recommended City Council acceptance of a $132,000 Massachusetts Downtown Initiative Capital Grant to refresh and strengthen the Harbor Walk, by a 2-1 vote with Councilor Page opposed.
Recommended City Council acceptance of a $124,300 Housing Choice Grant for the Railroad Ave 40R project, by a 2-0 vote with Councilor Page present and not voting.
Continued the Mass Cultural Council grant of $14,000 to the November 5, 2026 Budget meeting, with no vote taken.
Continued review of the City's FY2026 OPEB Actuarial Valuation Reports to November 5, 2026.

1. Memorandum from the Principal Assessor regarding tax classification (cont. from October 7, 
2026)
Summary of Discussion: Principal Assessor, Nancy Papows stated that the Department of Revenue
had approved the City’s assessed values and new growth, which allowed the City to move forward with
the tax classification process. She stated that there were no new parcels classified as open space, and the
mayor had decided not to adopt either the residential or small commercial exemption, the focus would be
on whether to shift a portion of the tax levy from one class of property to another. 
Nancy Papows stated that the Residential tax class made up 91.7% of the total, while the commercial
industrial, and personal property made up 8.3%. She stated that the taxable value of the city increased
close to 7% and the Residential tax class increased 6.5%.
Assessor, Tim Good shared his screen.
Budget & Finance                               October 22, 2026                                     Page 2 of 12
Nancy Papows stated the above. She stated that a tax factor of 1 would result in the same tax rate for all
classes of property, while any other number would shift a portion of the levy to another class.
Budget & Finance                               October 22, 2026                                     Page 3 of 12
Budget & Finance                               October 22, 2026                                     Page 4 of 12
Nancy Papows stated the above.
Budget & Finance                               October 22, 2026                                     Page 5 of 12
Nancy Papows stated the above. She stated that at a shift of 1.03 the annual saving to a resident would
be $15, while for a Commercial, Industrial, and Personal taxpayer would pay an additional $210. She
stated the maximum shift, which would save the residential taxpayer $300, while the commercial,
industrial, and property taxpayer would pay just over $3,400 more.
Councilor Grow stated that while he believed parity between the tax classes should exist, the increasing
share of Residential property meant that Residential tax payers would not see substantial savings if a tax
shift was made in their favor. 
Councilor Memhard stated that he agreed the tax factor should be 1.0 to create a balanced tax levy, but
there was a large differential between tax classes. 
Councilor Memhard asked what the Mayor’s recommendation was. Nancy Papows stated that she had
spoken with the mayor and he recommended a 1.03 CIP shift.
Councilor Page stated that the rate should stay as it had been the previous fiscal year.

7. Memorandum from the Director of Community Development requesting the Massachusetts 
Downtown Initiative Capital Grant from the Commonwealth’s Executive Office of Economic 
Development in the amount of $132,000
Summary of Discussion: Community Development Director, Alex Koppelman stated that improving
the Harbor Walk has been a longstanding priority for multiple administrations. He stated that the City
had previously received American Rescue Plan Act funding from the Federal government and listening
sessions had been conducted to decide how those funds would be spent, with a portion of the funds being
dedicated to wayfinding signs. He stated that the process had begun before he had joined the department,
and he had been working on how to implement the project. He stated that there would be no match to the
grant required by the City.
Economic Development Coordinator, Emily Sloan stated that a survey of downtown business owners
had been conducted the previous February which had determined that wayfinding was still an important
priority. She stated wayfinding improvements would help with accessibility within downtown and the
connectedness of downtown. She stated that improved wayfinding would also improve the walkability of
downtown. She stated that this grant would help fund installation of signage between the working
waterfront, Main Street, and the train station. She stated that the Harbor Walk had been installed in 2012
and the signs had a 10-year life span, which were now weathered and losing legibility. She stated that
while there was great information on the posts, it was not clear where the Harbor Walk actually went.
She stated that large directory style signs had recently installed, and there were several other signs that
would be installed, including directional signs. She stated that with the new round of funding, signs to
complement the existing signage would be installed. She stated that signs leading from the train station to
downtown would be prioritized. 
Arts, Culture & Events Coordinator, Miranda Aisling Hynes stated that the current locations of the
Harbor Walk granite posts would remain the same, but the signs would be reinstalled with small updates
to the content. She stated that she would be working with the art community to design sidewalk trail
markers. She stated that the Harbor Walk had been designed with subtlety in mind and new sidewalk trail
markers would balance that subtlety with wayfinding. She stated that visual anchors a few feet in size
would be installed at key intersection along the Harbor Walk. She stated that these anchors would be
thermoplastic which would have a 10-year lifespan, which would last much longer than paint on a
sidewalk.
Budget & Finance                               October 22, 2026                                     Page 8 of 12
Councilor Page asked what these anchors would look like. Miranda Aisling Hynes stated that the
anchors would be designed via a public engagement process, and the design of these anchors would be
funded by this grant. 
Councilor Grow asked if the Committee for the Arts should be involved in the design of the anchors as
they would be public art. Miranda Aisling Hynes stated that they had not yet been involved as there had
been an embargo on the announcement of the grant funding until recently. She stated that the Harbortown
Cultural District had been informed and the Committee for the Arts would be involved as well. 
Councilor Grow asked if the QR codes on the Harbor Walk would be replaced. Miranda Aisling Hynes
stated that they had already been updated and they were all working.
Councilor Grow asked for clarification on the cost of the of the directory signs that had been installed.
Alex Koppelman stated that the signs were part of a larger initiative of placemaking that needed to be
done professionally. He stated that previous funding through ARPA had funded the design of the whole
sign family as well as create a map of locations. He stated that this was a complex process that required
an expert design firm. He stated the signs were large and made from very durable materials meant to last
a long period of time, and also needed to be able to withstand heavy winds since they were large. He
stated that the installation had been more complex and required outsourcing them. He stated that 90% of
the funding that had been used for the signs had been federally funded, and the funding from the City had
already been dedicated to tourism. Emily Sloan stated that the new round of signs would be a larger
number of small signs including over 100 for the Harbor Walk and the sidewalk anchors. 
Councilor Grow asked what the expected life span of the large directory signs was. Alex Koppelman
stated they were expected to last about twenty years.
Councilor Page stated she disagreed with the initial use of Community Block Grant funds for this project,
and that the directory sign on the boulevard was placed in an unideal location. 
Councilor Page stated that in the grant application it stated that the DPW would replace the signs when
needed, and had the burden on the DPW been considered. Emily Sloan stated that during the grant
application process the DPW had been consulted and they had agreed to replacing the signs. She stated
that the DPW regularly installed signs and felt comfortable working with these signs. 
Councilor Page stated that the signs currently were oriented in such a way that they pointed away from
downtown not towards when facing the signs. Alex Koppelman stated that the signs were oriented to
true north, and the designer had opted for consistency based on that. He stated that a compass had been
proposed in some designs. Councilor Grow stated that he agreed that the orientation seemed to be
backwards. 
Councilor Page requested that the owners of boats, which were small businesses, be included in outreach.
Councilor Page stated that better signage for public restrooms was important throughout the downtown
area. 
Councilor Grow asked if self-cleaning toilets in the European style had ever been considered.
Councilor Memhard stated that public restrooms downtown had been an ongoing issue. Alex
Koppelman stated that only City owned public restrooms had been identified on the new signage.
Budget & Finance                               October 22, 2026                                     Page 9 of 12
Councilor Page asked for clarification regarding proposed use of CDBG funds for ongoing maintenance
of the signs. Alex Koppelman stated that CDBG funding was reliable ongoing funding, but other funding
sources would be explored as well. 
Councilor Page asked for clarification regarding metrics that would be tracked. Emily Sloan stated that
some statistics had been reported during the application process, but other statistics would be tracked
such as downtown foot traffic, website visits, and number of times QR codes were used. 
Councilor Grow asked if the Chamber of Commerce had been asked to help with funding maintenance
of the signs since they would directly impact their membership. Emily Sloan stated that they had not so
far, but had contributed in other ways. 
Councilor Grow stated that the grant application process was complicated and in depth, and provided
the City millions of dollars in funding that was outside of the budget. 
Councilor Page read the following statement:
“These actions are not isolated but inter-related.
I would like to thank CC President Gross for honoring my request to be appointed as the CC liaison to
the Fisheries Commission. My life's work has been in fisheries. I am here today to defend the working
waterfront.
Now to the issue at hand. We are here to consider a $132k State grant more wayfinding signs ($33,800),
enhancements to the Harbor Walk, and public art etc. Are there preliminary plans? Any specifics? The
grant application was not provided to us for our consideration. There is no clear idea of what is being 
recommended. We'll find out when installation arrives.
St. Peter's COMMERCIAL Marina docks vessels of relatively small size. With an early October storm
predicted, lobstermen made the prudent decision to begin removing gear and bringing it in for winter
storage. Deciding to bring in gear early, saves potential loss of gear (reducing ghost gear) thus mitigating
financial loss and ensures the SAFETY of captain and crew. Lobstermen began storing gear on the City's
designated area on the dock. Note, prior to the granite benches there now, there were wooden benches
located much closer to the railing. Traps need to be stored behind these rows of benches. The granite
benches were installed further back resulting in less trap storage. Dominic #1.
State Ch.91 licenses do not limit use by setting dates. The control dates for trap storage are arbitrarily set
by the Municipality. Article VI, states traps shall be permitted between November 15th and May 15th.
The Harbormasters office issued an edict to each vessel docked at St. Peter's - remove all traps from the
city's dock prior to November 15th. No other instruction or explanation.
We are fortunate to have received a $2.7 million SEC grant which required $700k in local funding. This
funding will completely renovate St. Peter's Commercial Marina and the public landing. We are excited
to have this critical piece of working waterfront infrastructure upgraded. However, what is missing? No
hoist you say? I vehemently objected to the fact that a working hoist would not be part of this
infrastructure upgrade. Such a hoist is for light duty as only lobster traps and bait are transferred from
shore to the water sheet here. Do not listen to the naysayers, this can't be accomplished. Of course it can.
A slight readjustment of the public landing makes way for &. hoist. This public landing is an
encroachment within the MI/DPA being service for recreational vessels. Without a hoist, nothing grounds
the project to commercial working waterfront uses, but serves as a generic, gentrified investment with
potential to easily flip to recreational use in the future.
Budget & Finance                               October 22, 2026                                     Page 10 of 12
I am aware there is chatter the new decking couldn't possibly be used for gear/ trap storage any longer as
gear storage will serve to prematurely erode this new precious decking. Well folks, that's why it's called
a WORKING waterfront. It's hardcore, messy at times and yes takes wear and tear.
In the same round of SEC awards, Beverly, MA received a $500k grant. Beverly is investing in a hoist
on their working waterfront. I know this marina well. I was raised on this property. My grandfather,
Anthony F. Pizzella, built and operated this marina. The property was seized in a dual State and Municipal
eminent domain taking in the early 1980's. But I digress.
Given what I present here, I am skeptical these Harbor Walk "improvements" will support or improve the
working waterfront, yet serve to further chip away, further impede the fishermen and complete the
gentrification. I will not stand by as they replace our working waterfront and the fishermen with fairies
in the in the Nation's oldest fishing port.”
There was a brief discussion regarding the hoist that had been formally at St. Peter’s Park.
COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATION: On a motion by Councilor Memhard, seconded by Councilor 
Page, the Budget & Finance Committee voted 2 in favor, 1 opposed (Page), to recommend that the City 
Council accept under MGL c. 44, §53A, a state grant from the Mass. Executive Office of Economic 
Development, Massachusetts Downtown Initiative Capital Grant in the amount of $132,000 for the 
purpose of refreshing and strengthening the Harbor Walk. There are no local matching requirements for
the grant and the period is from January 1, 2027 through April 30, 2028.
8. Memorandum from the Director of Community Development requesting the Housing Choice 
Grant from the Massachusetts Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities in the 
amount of $124,300 
Summary of Discussion: Alex Koppelman stated that this funding would allow for one of the main
recommendations in the City Housing Compass Plan to be implemented. He stated that this grant would
provide funding for technical assistance for the planning-level analysis of traffic and infrastructure needs
for the 7 Railroad Avenue site. He stated that the goal was to make the area more viable for the return of
a grocery store to the site, and mixed-use housing would play a critical role in that. 
Councilor Memhard asked if the property owners needed to be involved in the matter. Alex Koppelman
stated that during this process there would be community engagement and the owner of 7 Railroad
Avenue had been engaged throughout the process already and that engagement would continue. 
Councilor Grow asked what would be the end product of this grant. Alex Koppelman stated that this
grant funding would be used to create Smart Growth Zoning on Railroad Avenue, and it would be used
to hire a consultant who would help draft zoning and work through the process with the State, as well as
engage the community. 
Councilor Grow asked if the property owner had to be receptive to these zoning changes before they
were implemented. Alex Koppelman stated that it was important to work with the property owner,
though zoning did not compel the owner to do anything it just gave them the option. 
Councilor Grow asked if the inclusion of a grocery store in any future development would be involved
in this zoning. Alex Koppelman stated that a condition of the zoning could be that a grocery store was
included, but outreach would need to be done to help make that happen. He stated that by including
housing in future development it would make for a stronger market for a grocery store.
Budget & Finance                               October 22, 2026                                     Page 11 of 12
Councilor Memhard stated that building a new space to the specifications of a grocery partner would
help draw one in.
Councilor Page asked if the new zoning would have to be a contiguous area. Alex Koppelman stated
that the boundaries of the zoning would be decided through this process. 
COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATION: On a motion by Councilor Memhard, seconded by Councilor
Page, the Budget & Finance Committee voted, 2 in favor, 0 opposed, 1 present (Page), to recommend
that the City Council accept under MGL c. 44, §53A, a state grant from the Mass. Executive Office of
Housing & Livable Communities, Housing Choice Grant Program in the amount of $124,300 for the
purpose of the Railroad Ave 40R project. There is a $12,500 local matching requirement for grant and
the grant period is from January 1, 2027 through June 30, 2028.
9. Memorandum from the Arts, Culture and Events Coordinator requesting acceptance of the 
Mass Cultural Council Grant in the amount of $14,000
Summary of Discussion: Miranda Aisling Hynes stated that this funding was based on an algorithm
based on municipality size, population, and other metrics. She stated that the funds were granted to the
Gloucester Cultural Council which used the funds to issue smaller grants directly to organizations or
artists. 
Councilor Grow asked how much were the micro-grants that the Gloucester Cultural Council gave out.
Miranda Aisling Hynes stated that they were between $200 and $1,000 generally.
Councilor Page asked how the funds would be spent. Miranda Aisling Hynes stated that it would
depend on the applications received by the Gloucester Cultural Council, and that there had been about 40
received. 
There was no vote taken, and this matter was continued to the November 5, 2026 Budget meeting.
10. Memorandum from the City Auditor regarding accounts having expenditures which exceed
their authorization & Auditor’s Report and other related business
Summary of Discussion: Auditor, Kenny Costa stated that there were 18 accounts in deficit. He stated
that there was a $23,000 increase since last report. He stated that this year deficits were being cleared
during the fiscal year rather than waiting to the close of the year. 
No motion offered.
MOTION: On a motion by Councilor Grow, seconded by Councilor Page, the Budget & Finance
Committee voted, 3 in favor, 0 opposed, to adjourn at 6:57 p.m.

**7. Memorandum from the Director of Community Development requesting the Massachusetts Downtown Initiative Capital Grant from the Commonwealth’s Executive Office of Economic Development in the amount of $132,000**

**Summary of Discussion:** **Community Development Director, Alex Koppelman** stated that improving the Harbor Walk has been a longstanding priority for multiple administrations. He stated that the City had previously received American Rescue Plan Act funding from the Federal government and listening sessions had been conducted to decide how those funds would be spent, with a portion of the funds being dedicated to wayfinding signs. He stated that the process had begun before he had joined the department, and he had been working on how to implement the project. He stated that there would be no match to the grant required by the City.

**Economic Development Coordinator, Emily Sloan** stated that a survey of downtown business owners had been conducted the previous February which had determined that wayfinding was still an important priority. She stated wayfinding improvements would help with accessibility within downtown and the connectedness of downtown. She stated that improved wayfinding would also improve the walkability of downtown. She stated that this grant would help fund installation of signage between the working waterfront, Main Street, and the train station. She stated that the Harbor Walk had been installed in 2012 and the signs had a 10-year life span, which were now weathered and losing legibility. She stated that while there was great information on the posts, it was not clear where the Harbor Walk actually went. She stated that large directory style signs had recently installed, and there were several other signs that would be installed, including directional signs. She stated that with the new round of funding, signs to complement the existing signage would be installed. She stated that signs leading from the train station to downtown would be prioritized.

**Arts, Culture & Events Coordinator, Miranda Aisling Hynes** stated that the current locations of the Harbor Walk granite posts would remain the same, but the signs would be reinstalled with small updates to the content. She stated that she would be working with the art community to design sidewalk trail markers. She stated that the Harbor Walk had been designed with subtlety in mind and new sidewalk trail markers would balance that subtlety with wayfinding. She stated that visual anchors a few feet in size would be installed at key intersection along the Harbor Walk. She stated that these anchors would be thermoplastic which would have a 10-year lifespan, which would last much longer than paint on a sidewalk.

**Councilor Page** asked what these anchors would look like. **Miranda Aisling Hynes** stated that the anchors would be designed via a public engagement process, and the design of these anchors would be funded by this grant.

**Councilor Grow** asked if the Committee for the Arts should be involved in the design of the anchors as they would be public art. **Miranda Aisling Hynes** stated that they had not yet been involved as there had been an embargo on the announcement of the grant funding until recently. She stated that the Harbortown Cultural District had been informed and the Committee for the Arts would be involved as well.

**Councilor Grow** asked if the QR codes on the Harbor Walk would be replaced. **Miranda Aisling Hynes** stated that they had already been updated and they were all working.

**Councilor Grow** asked for clarification on the cost of the of the directory signs that had been installed. **Alex Koppelman** stated that the signs were part of a larger initiative of placemaking that needed to be done professionally. He stated that previous funding through ARPA had funded the design of the whole sign family as well as create a map of locations. He stated that this was a complex process that required an expert design firm. He stated the signs were large and made from very durable materials meant to last a long period of time, and also needed to be able to withstand heavy winds since they were large. He stated that the installation had been more complex and required outsourcing them. He stated that 90% of the funding that had been used for the signs had been federally funded, and the funding from the City had already been dedicated to tourism. **Emily Sloan** stated that the new round of signs would be a larger number of small signs including over 100 for the Harbor Walk and the sidewalk anchors.

**Councilor Grow** asked what the expected life span of the large directory signs was. **Alex Koppelman** stated they were expected to last about twenty years.

**Councilor Page** stated she disagreed with the initial use of Community Block Grant funds for this project, and that the directory sign on the boulevard was placed in an unideal location.

**Councilor Page** stated that in the grant application it stated that the DPW would replace the signs when needed, and had the burden on the DPW been considered. **Emily Sloan** stated that during the grant application process the DPW had been consulted and they had agreed to replacing the signs. She stated that the DPW regularly installed signs and felt comfortable working with these signs.

**Councilor Page** stated that the signs currently were oriented in such a way that they pointed away from downtown not towards when facing the signs. **Alex Koppelman** stated that the signs were oriented to true north, and the designer had opted for consistency based on that. He stated that a compass had been proposed in some designs. **Councilor Grow** stated that he agreed that the orientation seemed to be backwards.

**Councilor Page** requested that the owners of boats, which were small businesses, be included in outreach.

**Councilor Page** stated that better signage for public restrooms was important throughout the downtown area.

**Councilor Grow** asked if self-cleaning toilets in the European style had ever been considered.

**Councilor Memhard** stated that public restrooms downtown had been an ongoing issue. **Alex Koppelman** stated that only City owned public restrooms had been identified on the new signage.

**Councilor Page** asked for clarification regarding proposed use of CDBG funds for ongoing maintenance of the signs. **Alex Koppelman** stated that CDBG funding was reliable ongoing funding, but other funding sources would be explored as well.

**Councilor Page** asked for clarification regarding metrics that would be tracked. **Emily Sloan** stated that some statistics had been reported during the application process, but other statistics would be tracked such as downtown foot traffic, website visits, and number of times QR codes were used.

**Councilor Grow** asked if the Chamber of Commerce had been asked to help with funding maintenance of the signs since they would directly impact their membership. **Emily Sloan** stated that they had not so far, but had contributed in other ways.

**Councilor Grow** stated that the grant application process was complicated and in depth, and provided the City millions of dollars in funding that was outside of the budget.

**Councilor Page** read the following statement:

> “These actions are not isolated but inter-related.
>

**8. Memorandum from the Director of Community Development requesting the Housing Choice Grant from the Massachusetts Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities in the amount of $124,300**

**Summary of Discussion:** **Alex Koppelman** stated that this funding would allow for one of the main recommendations in the City Housing Compass Plan to be implemented. He stated that this grant would provide funding for technical assistance for the planning-level analysis of traffic and infrastructure needs for the 7 Railroad Avenue site. He stated that the goal was to make the area more viable for the return of a grocery store to the site, and mixed-use housing would play a critical role in that.

**Councilor Memhard** asked if the property owners needed to be involved in the matter. **Alex Koppelman** stated that during this process there would be community engagement and the owner of 7 Railroad Avenue had been engaged throughout the process already and that engagement would continue.

**Councilor Grow** asked what would be the end product of this grant. **Alex Koppelman** stated that this grant funding would be used to create Smart Growth Zoning on Railroad Avenue, and it would be used to hire a consultant who would help draft zoning and work through the process with the State, as well as engage the community.

**Councilor Grow** asked if the property owner had to be receptive to these zoning changes before they were implemented. **Alex Koppelman** stated that it was important to work with the property owner, though zoning did not compel the owner to do anything it just gave them the option.

**Councilor Grow** asked if the inclusion of a grocery store in any future development would be involved in this zoning. **Alex Koppelman** stated that a condition of the zoning could be that a grocery store was included, but outreach would need to be done to help make that happen. He stated that by including housing in future development it would make for a stronger market for a grocery store.

**Councilor Memhard** stated that building a new space to the specifications of a grocery partner would help draw one in.

**Councilor Page** asked if the new zoning would have to be a contiguous area. **Alex Koppelman** stated that the boundaries of the zoning would be decided through this process.

COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATION: On a motion by Councilor Memhard, seconded by Councilor Page, the Budget & Finance Committee voted, 2 in favor, 0 opposed, 1 present (Page), to recommend that the City Council accept under MGL c. 44, §53A, a state grant from the Mass. Executive Office of Housing & Livable Communities, Housing Choice Grant Program in the amount of $124,300 for the purpose of the Railroad Ave 40R project.
